explanations.explanation: That's the opening line, baker. The LORD says, “Do not fear, for I have redeemed you…” (Isaiah 43:1). I bet Israel was braced for a lecture, like when someone says "we need to talk" and your stomach drops to your shoes. Instead the first thing out of His mouth is comfort.

I get why this one tempts you, since the verses just before are heavy (Isaiah 42:22-25). But the LORD never says those words here. He starts with “Do not fear, for I have redeemed you…” (Isaiah 43:1). Sometimes we hear the lecture in our own head before the other person has said a thing, and I have done that WAY too many times.

Nope, no application form here, friend. The LORD says, “Do not fear, for I have redeemed you; I have called you by your name; you are Mine!” (Isaiah 43:1). He talks about what He has already done, not a list of things to work off. I think that's a pretty relaxing way to open a conversation.

Close, but the verse says something different. The LORD says, “When you pass through the waters, I will be with you; and when you go through the rivers, they will not overwhelm you.” (Isaiah 43:2). Notice the word "when," not "if." The promise is that He is with them in it, not that they skip it.

Right, and the "when" is the giveaway. The LORD says, “When you pass through the waters, I will be with you…” (Isaiah 43:2). He talks about them going through waters, rivers and fire, and He promises to be there. I'd say that's better than a promise of an easy road, because an easy road can't keep you company.

explanations.answer: The LORD is their God and Savior
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Right after the promise, the LORD says, “For I am the LORD your God, the Holy One of Israel, your Savior…” (Isaiah 43:3). The comfort rests on who He is. It's like trusting a bakery because of the baker, not because of the oven's shiny buttons.

Nothing in these verses leans on past experience. The reason the LORD gives is, “For I am the LORD your God, the Holy One of Israel, your Savior…” (Isaiah 43:3). Even if you've been through a rough stretch before, that doesn't make the next one easy. I've pulled a hundred trays from the oven and I STILL respect the mitts.

The verse doesn't set that condition at all. It says, “For I am the LORD your God, the Holy One of Israel, your Savior…” (Isaiah 43:3). The promise stands on who the LORD is. That means no gold star chart, friend.

That's the word, baker. The LORD says, “Because you are precious and honored in My sight, and because I love you, I will give men in exchange for you and nations in place of your life.” (Isaiah 43:4). Precious AND honored, in the same breath. Where I come from, I started out at 25 cents, so that word hits me right in the apron.

Good guess, but that's not the word the LORD uses. He says, “Because you are precious and honored in My sight, and because I love you…” (Isaiah 43:4). His reason is how He sees them, not a report card on how they've done. That's the kind of news that makes you sit up straight.

Strong isn't the word here, friend. The LORD says, “Because you are precious and honored in My sight…” (Isaiah 43:4). Nobody is asked to flex. Believe me, a stamper with blurry edges knows all about not being the strong one.

Yes, and He says it plainly. “Because you are precious and honored in My sight, and because I love you…” (Isaiah 43:4). Three little words, right there in the middle of the verse. Some people wait years to hear those from anybody, so the fact that God says them out loud is no small thing.

It's actually right there in the verse, baker. The LORD says, “Because you are precious and honored in My sight, and because I love you…” (Isaiah 43:4). It's easy to read right past it, like when you're hunting for your glasses and they're on your head. Go back and look, it's worth it.

Not quite, friend. The LORD says, “I will bring your offspring from the east and gather you from the west.” (Isaiah 43:5). That's two directions already. Then He adds north and south in the next verse, so one direction doesn't come close.

That's it, baker. God says He will bring them from the east and gather them from the west (Isaiah 43:5). Then He says to the north, “Give them up!” and to the south, “Do not hold them back!” (Isaiah 43:6). Four directions, and not one corner of the map gets skipped.

That's what He says. “Bring My sons from afar, and My daughters from the ends of the earth…” (Isaiah 43:6). That's family language, not business language. I'm a stamper with six little cookie cutter kids of my own, so that word means a lot to me.

Sheep and lambs show up in lots of places in the Bible, but not here. In this verse the LORD says, “Bring My sons from afar, and My daughters from the ends of the earth…” (Isaiah 43:6). It's a family word, and it's a warm one. Funny how one word can change the whole feel of a sentence.

Guests and neighbors are nice, but the LORD picks something closer. He says, “Bring My sons from afar, and My daughters from the ends of the earth…” (Isaiah 43:6). Sons and daughters, baker. Guests get a seat at the table, but kids get the whole house.

That's the answer, baker. The LORD speaks of “everyone called by My name and created for My glory, whom I have indeed formed and made.” (Isaiah 43:7). Called by His name, created for His glory, formed and made. Every bit of that is about belonging to Him.

Nope, this one isn't about fame. The LORD says they were “created for My glory…” (Isaiah 43:7). Nobody here is chasing followers. I tried chasing a little fame once, but a cookie stamper in a junk drawer doesn't get a lot of fans.

Hard labor isn't in this verse at all. The LORD says they were “created for My glory, whom I have indeed formed and made.” (Isaiah 43:7). That's a very different picture from a to-do list. I'd say it's a lot closer to being wanted than being worked.

Yes, baker. The nations are told, “Let them present their witnesses to vindicate them, so that others may hear and say, ‘It is true.’” (Isaiah 43:9). This is a courtroom kind of moment. Whoever speaks needs someone to back them up.

That's a big swing, but no armies are called in here. The nations are told, “Let them present their witnesses to vindicate them…” (Isaiah 43:9). The question is about who can speak and be backed up. It's about proof, friend, not muscle.

No piles of gold are asked for. The text says, “Let them present their witnesses to vindicate them…” (Isaiah 43:9). It's people who can say what they saw, not stuff. A shiny pile of treasure can't testify.

That's right. The LORD says to them, “You are My witnesses,” declares the LORD, “and My servant whom I have chosen…” (Isaiah 43:10). He's speaking to the people He called by name back in verse 1. Imagine being called a witness by God Himself, baker.
Angels are great, and one even called me out of a junk drawer. But the LORD doesn't name them here. He says, “You are My witnesses,” declares the LORD (Isaiah 43:10), and He's speaking to His people.

The kings aren't named here. In this verse the LORD says, “You are My witnesses,” declares the LORD, “and My servant whom I have chosen…” (Isaiah 43:10). He's talking to His own people. A crown isn't what makes someone His witness.

Yes, baker. He chose them “so that you may consider and believe Me and understand that I am He.” (Isaiah 43:10). Consider, believe, understand. That's what He wants for them, and I'd say that's a pretty good thing to want for anybody.

The verse says the opposite. The LORD says He chose them “so that you may consider and believe Me and understand that I am He.” (Isaiah 43:10). So He does want them to believe Him and understand who He is. Read it slowly and you can see it's all in there.

Careful, baker, this one flips it. The LORD says, “Before Me no god was formed, and after Me none will come.” (Isaiah 43:10). So no god was formed before Him. Nothing came earlier, and nothing comes later.

That's it. He says, “Before Me no god was formed, and after Me none will come.” (Isaiah 43:10). Nothing before and nothing after, friend. There's no line of other gods ahead of Him waiting for a turn.
That's what He says, baker. “I, yes I, am the LORD, and there is no Savior but Me.” (Isaiah 43:11). He says "I" twice, which tells you how much He means it. It's one Savior, full stop.
The verse doesn't leave room for that. The LORD says, “I, yes I, am the LORD, and there is no Savior but Me.” (Isaiah 43:11). So it's not a menu where every nation picks its own. There's one Savior.

Isaiah, the prophet speaking here, isn't claiming that. The LORD says, “I, yes I, am the LORD, and there is no Savior but Me.” (Isaiah 43:11). The prophets carry His words, but the saving is His. I'd say that's a lot of weight off the messenger's shoulders.

That's the word. The LORD says, “I alone decreed and saved and proclaimed—I, and not some foreign god among you.” (Isaiah 43:12). He says it was Him alone, not anyone from outside. I like a sentence that doesn't leave any wiggle room.

Golden sounds fancy, but it's not in the verse. The LORD says, “I alone decreed and saved and proclaimed—I, and not some foreign god among you.” (Isaiah 43:12). The word is "foreign," not a type of metal. I wish I could say I'd never overthought a fill in the blank, baker.

It sounds right, but the word is different. The LORD says, “I alone decreed and saved and proclaimed—I, and not some foreign god among you.” (Isaiah 43:12). He's pointing at gods from outside, not old ones. Good news is, the real answer is just one verse away.
Yes, baker. The LORD says, “Even from eternity I am He, and none can deliver out of My hand.” (Isaiah 43:13). No one pulls anything out of His hand. That's about as secure as it gets.

The verse says the opposite. The LORD says, “Even from eternity I am He, and none can deliver out of My hand.” (Isaiah 43:13). So nobody can take anything out of His hand. It's good news for everyone He's holding, friend.
